9. Nominalizations - turning processes into nouns, so instead of describing exactly how to do something, you just say the noun for the process, like "healing" or "safety" or "trust" or "integration" or "communion" or "clarity" or "rest" or whatever. This is vague, which is sometimes useful because the subconscious will concretize it in a way that works.
Your body knows how to make you feel a little bit safer in a way that works for you.

10. Questions from the Meta Model - the de-hypnosis tool. Just as you need both the Milton Model and the Meta Model for ethical NLP, you need both for ethical hypnosis. So when you want to zero in on what's really true, just ask questions like

How specifically? According to whom? Compared to what? Is that always true? Have there been times when it wasn't? Is that never false? What specifically would happen? How do you know that? How could you tell? What evidence would convince you otherwise?
and so on. So, you can use the Milton Model to let yourself be softened by hypnosis, and the Meta Model to make sure you're always coming back to what's true.
There are also some other tools from NLP that are useful in hypnosis, like working with sensory qualities, state management, and strategies.

Working with submodalities is an extremely powerful tool, but it can be risky if you're working with something like fear or craving or fantasy or a belief or a memory. Before you start, first notice the sensory qualities - is it near or far, bright or dim, loud or quiet, moving or still, heavy or light, inside or outside your body, etc. If you don't notice any, just don't use this tool.
How is that being represented in your mind? How could you change that representation to make it more useful to you?
I'm not deleting that, I'm just changing the volume so I can listen without being overwhelmed.
Before you change the submodalities, it's a good idea to ask the guard if that's okay.
Is it okay if I move that image back a little, and turn the volume down a little, so that I can still be present and listen to what you have to say?

Anchoring can also be useful - you can use a physical gesture (putting your hand on your heart, touching two fingers together, etc.) or a breath or a word or a posture or a scent or a song or whatever. To create an anchor, first find a state that you want an anchor for. When you're in that state, apply the anchor and say "this is available to you". If you're anchoring a way to go back into hypnosis, don't go for the peak of the emotional state, but instead use a state that's actually useful to you where you're receptive to hypnosis (see the main induction section, "A shortcut back into hypnosis"). You can also anchor a way to be both alert and calm, and you can anchor a way to wake up using synchronicity (see below).

I've talked before about synchronicity . One of the problems is that when you notice one, you usually want to figure out what it means, and that can lead to finding patterns everywhere, often compulsively. One way to deal with this is to use noticing synchronicity as a wake-up bell. It doesn't necessarily mean anything, it just catches your attention, and that's all you need.
Anchor a wake-up routine for whenever you notice a synchronicity. The script might be:

Whenever I notice a synchronicity, it can wake me up out of whatever state I'm in. I can feel my body, feel the room I'm in, and remember that the synchronicity doesn't actually mean anything. I can expand my focus to be broader than whatever state I'm currently in. I can consider what's actually true, separate from my current emotional state. I can see what needs nurturing, what needs protection, what needs action, from my highest perspective, while still being in my body, in the real world, surrounded by other human beings. I can access whatever state is useful to me - objectivity, clarity, ease, peace, freedom, joy, gratitude, etc.
So when you notice a synchronicity, you pause, orient yourself, expand your focus, reality test, listen to whatever you need to listen to, and then take one useful action from love.

That way, you're not being swept up in the state, but you're still able to see if there's something the inner child wants, or something a Protector wants to tell you, or something you need to grieve, or something that's wrong in your body, or something you need to act on.

To install this anchor, imagine noticing a synchronicity - it doesn't have to be a special one, just imagine noticing one. Notice the "whoa" moment, when you realize that you noticed the synchronicity. At that point, feel your feet on the floor, feel your whole body, take a breath, feel the room, and repeat to yourself that noticing the synchronicity doesn't mean it has a message for you, but it is a wake-up bell. Then do whatever you want to do to wake up - ask your Nurturer what it sees, ask your Protector, ask your Leader, etc. Practice getting back to a more grounded state, with a broader perspective. Then, take one action, and fully exit hypnosis, waking up completely.
That way, the anchor is under your control, visible to you, revocable, and narrowly-focused.

This is similar to what in psychology is called implementation intentions . I haven't seen anyone using synchronicity as a cue for an implementation intention, but the general idea has been studied, and there's good evidence that it works (starting with this paper by Gollwitzer).

The problem is that the same mechanism which makes this technique powerful, makes it potentially dangerous. Just like an alien abduction implant, if you rehearse that a synchronicity is a cue, your brain may start scanning for that cue, and if you are particularly suggestible, absorbable, or destabilizable, you may start to see patterns where there are none and interpret them to have a meaning that they don't. Research shows that the same part of the brain that sees patterns, sees patterns where there are none leading to false positive interpretations, and this trait is correlated with psychosis spectrum traits. (See Blain et al. and Grant et al.)

If you find that this technique makes you scan for patterns, lose sleep, feel anxious, think that random occurrences are meaningful, or in any other way, make it harder to distinguish what is really meaningful from what is not, you should deactivate this technique.

You can deactivate this technique by simply stopping the rehearsal of this technique, and saying in a fully awake state, "Seeing synchronicities is no longer going to be a cue for me, I'm releasing that association now." Then simply remove it from your list and stop rehearsing it.

Reframe: Rather than reframing in the way that some NLP trainings suggest, where you take what you think is a bad thing and convince yourself that it was good all along (lying to yourself is never helpful), I prefer to reframe by asking, "What else could be true?" or "Why might this be a good thing?" or to ask other parts of myself like the Nurturer, Protector, and Leader how to reframe it.

Perceptual Positions: Sometimes, I can't see something in a new way until I see it from someone else's point of view, so I put myself in the other person's shoes and see how they might perceive the situation. I also try looking at it from a third person's perspective or the perspective of the universal heart.

Future Pace: After you think you've learned something, think about the situations where you're likely to be tested on what you've learned, and imagine yourself in that situation. Imagine the cue that will trigger the behavior coming up, and then rehearse doing the thing you want to do. "If I see x, I'm going to do y." Keep it simple.
Swish Pattern: This is a classic NLP technique for getting yourself to visualize yourself in a new way rather than an old way.
Parts Integration: When two parts of you are in conflict, figure out what each part wants, then figure out if there's a way to meet both of their needs, or find a third option that does.

old: Daydreaming can be intuition, simulation, grief digestion, creative rehearsal, symbolic teaching, or the subconscious showing a possible future, fear, or desire. It can also become avoidance, fantasy addiction, dissociation, romantic obsession, or an escape hatch from adult life.
Does the daydream return me to life with more clarity, love, and action? Or does it pull me away from life into repetition, craving, and avoidance?
When it seems useful, ask:
“What is the guidance inside this?”
When it seems to be pulling you away, change the body before debating the story. Sit upright. Open the eyes a little. Feel the feet.

“Subconscious, thank you for showing me images. If this daydream is useful, please reveal the guidance inside it. If it is avoidance, please bring me gently into the present and help me deal with what I need to deal with in a gentle but structured way.”
Then get embarrassingly practical:
“What real-life action is this daydream replacing?”

new: Sometimes, daydreaming is intuitive. Your subconscious is simulating an idea or event to help you digest trauma or teach you something. If it’s helping you, ask for more specific guidance.

Then ask yourself, “What do I need to do in the real world that I’m avoiding by daydreaming?”

Ask around about what sort of training they have with what sorts of issues, how they use hypnosis, etc. If they are working with trauma, make sure they are trained in trauma and dissociation, not just hypnosis. Look at their credentials, etc., but know that even those are not a guarantee of how good they are.

On Forgiveness, a Paradox or Three (Why not to Bypass)

You can’t force yourself to forgive; you have to understand first. But trying to force yourself to forgive is bypassing, just as staying angry forever is bypassing. You can hold all these paradoxes at once: it was wrong, you still need to hold a boundary with the person, they still need to be accountable for it, and you may or may not forgive them later.

You may come to understand the person better, their conditioning, their history, their pain, their limitations, etc. and be able to understand that, given the total sum of who they were at the time, this is the only way they could have acted. That doesn’t make it right; they still need to be accountable and face the consequences of their actions and work on becoming someone who can act differently. You can still understand their limitations and have appropriate expectations for them.
I will not use spirituality to force you to forgive when you are not ready, but I will also not let you make your entire life around not forgiving.

What do I do if this happens?

First thing to do when you experience a demon, jinn, or other kind of hostile or intrusive presence is to do all of the normal things you would do when you encounter any part: check yourself for medical issues, check your environment, check your body, make sure you’re not overstimulated, and make sure your mind isn’t too open. “Right now, the only thing I want to deal with is something I can integrate. I’m bringing my adult self into this experience and I’m going to make sure my body is as safe as it can be.”

Appendix J - Try a few inductions out: a quick guide library

This time, look over the induction sequence, decide if you want to try it and for what purpose, and start it if you wish. Note that if you are not getting good imagery with any of these, it is OK to imagine them in some other channel: hearing the words, feeling a rhythm or location, physical touch or movement, or even just "knowing" it is happening.

1) Stretching and relaxing. Feel yourself supported and conscious of a limb (hand or foot are easiest). Stretch it out a little and then feel it relaxing into the ground or other support. You can do this by physically moving, or by just imagining it. See what happens (you may feel a relaxation, tension, warmth, a change in your breathing, or nothing at all), and repeat with up to 3 different areas of your body, feeling yourself letting go of whatever you need to let go of, perhaps asking yourself or the limb what it needs or what it has to say. Then return yourself to normal by moving your body as you choose, imagining moving, or some other way.

2) Floating. Notice yourself in your position, perhaps with eyes closed and supported. Imagine yourself floating up a bit, leaving only 1% of your effort to maintain contact with the support, and notice what happens. If you like, you can imagine yourself not floating, and maintain contact with the same weight and pressure you started with. You may wish to fractionate, by deliberately moving your attention to floating on an out breath, and back to your normal level of awareness on an in breath (note that you should tell yourself that this is what you're doing before you start doing it). Notice what you hear or experience at each level. Then deliberately drop yourself back to your chosen level of contact with the ground, feel your weight again, or ground yourself however you wish, and return.

3) Rhythmic breathing. You may use your breath, a hum, tapping a finger, outside rhythm, counting in your head, or even silence, or the deliberate lack of any rhythm. Pick a rhythm and repeat it a few times, perhaps saying to yourself (silently or aloud) "here, and here again". After a few times, deliberately stop doing the rhythm, and see if anything comes to mind when you hear the first silent or non-deliberate beat. Then return to your regular rhythm and return to normal.

4) Worry object. Imagine an object, such as a ball of yarn, perhaps representing a particular problem that has many strands. Unravel it in your mind's eye, or imagine blowing soap bubbles, or some other technique, and set aside each worry or strand where you can see it, perhaps saying its name or just counting it. Notice if there are any that need special care, and continue until you have only one left, or until you feel like stopping. You may also wish to name each part, or leave the object unchanged if you prefer. Then return to normal.

5) Journey. Hear your surroundings, feel your body, and then imagine walking to a place. You may wish to imagine the scene changing, or talk to someone there. Notice the mysterious unfolding of the scene, and then imagine returning along the same route.

6) Spreading wave. Imagine a small part of your body that is neutral to you, and notice what you feel or experience there. Then imagine a wave or spreading of that sensation to another part of your body, and notice what you experience there. (It is OK to imagine it not spreading, and just to keep it localized.) You may wish to repeat this for a few areas, but do not imagine yourself healing any medical conditions. You may wish to ask yourself what each area needs, or notice what happens as you go. The stories, arrangement and some details here are my own, as are the adaptations of the approaches described below. You don't need this open when you do this.
Learning, Entering and Returning

Adapted from Healing the Divided Self by Maggie Phillips and Claire Frederick (1995) pages 24-27, 45-50, 83-90 on interactive hypnosis, learning by the senses, self hypnosis and returning to full alertness in a definite way. It's a pro book not self-help, so it doesn't cover everything straightforwardly, and includes some procedures they do with each other that you probably shouldn't. On learning with and from yourself and other hypnostists and recordings see this ISH piece by Adam Eason and Benjamin Parris.

They use indirect techniques, described on pages 53-57 and 96-100, including pacing, utilization, metaphor and associational cues for re-entry. For discussion of those and other techniques see Nimja's hypnotic language tutorial and trigger tutorial . The language here is my own, adapted from those, and the sequence for returning, which is intentional, is likewise. Nimja neither wrote nor endorses this guide.

For body-oriented techniques see In an Unspoken Voice by Peter Levine (2010) ch 5, 7; Freedom from Pain by Levine and Maggie Phillips (2012) ch 3, 4; and Healing Trauma by Levine ch 4 for tracking and working with your body and its resources, titration, pendulation, paying attention to all the levels of sensation, image, behaviour, emotion, meaning.

For more on borrowed adulthoods, getting love without learning to trust it, making things right practically, spiritually, interpersonally, with other parts of you, dealing with spiritual bullshit, separating yourself out from other people, each other, and helping each other as peers, see the Inner Child Self-Love Reparenting Guide .

For more on renurturing, working with the body, and learning the capacities to nurture, see Healing the Divided Self pp148-153, 171-174; and Trauma Through a Child's Eyes by Levine and Maggie Kline, esp. ch 4-5, 10 for how to attune to and work with actual children, appreciating that they are different from each other and seeing what works when you're with someone who needs caring for. But the three-adult arrangement and borrowed-adulthood sequence are my own, and while those authors talk about working with parts, this is my adaptation of their ideas to that approach, not one they've done themselves.
Not everybody has an inner voice . Nedegard & Lupyan, 2024. The study isn't about adapting hypnosis, but the quick start contains some questions you can use to check.

On memory see Trauma and Memory by Levine (2015) ch 7. The VA has a page with cautions about hypnosis including strong reactions and false memories. The American Society of Clinical Hypnosis explains the difference between certification and competence. The links under evidence and finding a specialist are whatever they link to.
